case.case_title: Dissanayaka v. Superintendent Mahara Prison and Others
case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. (Spl.) 6/90, decided on 28 March 1991

clause.text: No person shall be arrested except according to law and must be informed of the reason.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the petitioner’s arrest was lawful and complied with Article 13(1) of the Constitution.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner claimed he was arrested on 08.03.1989 without being informed of the reason, was blindfolded, assaulted, and kept in unlawful custody initially at Galnewa Police Station.
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondents argued the petitioner was arrested on 04.04.89, not 08.03.89, and that the arrest was lawful under section 6(1) of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA) based on reasonable suspicion.
key_facts: Petitioner was arrested while trying to escape police during insurgent activity.
Petitioner was not informed of the reason for arrest and was blindfolded and assaulted.
Respondents claimed arrest was on 04.04.89 with authority under PTA.
No sufficient material was produced by the State to justify arrest beyond allegations.
Court found arrest lawful applying objective test despite lack of detailed evidence.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The Court held that Article 13(1) protects against arbitrary arrest and requires arrest to be lawful and reason for arrest to be given. The validity of arrest under PTA is judged by an objective test whether there was material for a reasonable officer to cause the arrest, not on proof of commission of offence.
reasoning.application_to_facts: Despite the petitioner’s claim of unlawful arrest and mistreatment, the Court found the arrest lawful because the petitioner was fleeing police during insurgent activity and the police had reasonable suspicion based on circumstances, even though the State did not produce detailed investigation notes.
principles_established: Arrest validity under Article 13(1) is determined by an objective test of reasonable suspicion.
The Court will not surrender its judgment to the executive; sufficient material must be placed before the Court.
During emergency, police have wider discretion but fundamental rights remain protected.
precedents_cited: Joseph Perera v. Attorney-General SC Nos 107-109/86
Somasiri v. Sub-Inspector Jayasena SC Application No. 147/88
Leelaratne v. Cyril Herat SC Nos. 144-145/86
Wickremabandu v. Cyril Herat SC Application No. 27/88
Sudath Silva v. Kodituwakku [1987] 2 Sri LR 119

outcome.holding: The Court held the petitioner’s arrest was lawful and not violative of Article 13(1) of the Constitution.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 13(1) was central to assessing the lawfulness of the petitioner’s arrest and whether the fundamental right against arbitrary arrest was infringed. The Court applied the objective test under this clause to uphold the arrest.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The Court found the arrest lawful because the petitioner was fleeing police during insurgent activity and the police had reasonable suspicion, despite lack of detailed investigation notes.
